plain_title: When sex hurts, or your body won't allow it
one_liner: Persistent pain, fear, or tightening of pelvic muscles with attempted penetration, causing distress, for six months or more.
in_simple_words: Genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder combines what used to be called vaginismus and dyspareunia. It involves pain during penetration, intense fear of that pain, or pelvic floor muscles tightening so penetration is difficult or impossible, with distress, for at least six months. It's not 'in your head'. Causes include skin and nerve conditions, infections, hormonal changes, childbirth injury, endometriosis, and learned muscle guarding after pain or fear. Treatment that combines physiotherapy and therapy works well.
what_it_can_feel_like: It felt like hitting a wall. For years I thought I was failing at something everyone else found easy.
Pelvic floor physio changed my life. Nobody had ever told me the muscles could learn to relax.
common_signs: Pain in the vulva, vagina, or pelvis during penetration or intercourse
Fear or anxiety about pain before, during, or after penetration
Pelvic floor muscles tightening so penetration is difficult or impossible
Lasting at least six months and causing distress
Often avoiding sex, tampons, or gynaecological exams

myths_vs_facts.myth: Painful sex is normal for women and something to put up with.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Pain is common but not normal, and it's treatable. Nobody should have to tolerate it.
There's usually a physical starting point, and the muscle guarding that follows is involuntary. Pelvic physiotherapy and therapy together treat both.

myths_vs_facts.myth: Having a drink first or pushing through will fix it.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Pushing through pain teaches the body to guard harder. Gradual, pain-free approaches work far better.

how_common.plain: Painful sex affects roughly 1 in 5 women at some point, and more after childbirth and around menopause. Severe muscle tightening (vaginismus) is less common but often undiagnosed.
how_common.figure: About 1 in 5 women experience painful sex (Jean Hailes); dyspareunia estimates 10%–15%, vaginismus 1%–2% in older surveys

what_helps.plain_summary: Assessment by a doctor or gynaecologist looks for treatable causes: infections, skin conditions, dryness after childbirth or at menopause, endometriosis, and nerve pain. Pelvic floor physiotherapy has the strongest evidence, teaching the muscles to relax and gradually restoring comfort, sometimes with graded trainers. Psychosexual therapy and CBT address fear, anxiety, and the relationship. Medical treatments target the underlying cause, prescribed and monitored by a doctor. Nothing should be forced or painful.
evidence_based_options: Psychosexual therapy and CBT for pain-related fear
Treatment of the physical cause (skin, hormones, infection, endometriosis)
Gradual, pain-free desensitisation guided by a clinician
self_help_that_supports_care: Stopping anything that hurts; pain is information, not a test
Lubricant, and time for arousal, if dryness is part of it
Telling your partner what's happening so it isn't misread

when_to_reach_out: If sex, tampons, or exams are painful or impossible, or fear of pain is stopping you, see a doctor, gynaecologist, or pelvic health physiotherapist. You don't have to prove it hurts; they'll believe you.
is_not: Sexual difficulties that are occasional, explained by a medical condition or medication, caused by severe relationship distress, or that don't bother you aren't diagnosed as a disorder. Pain from a single infection, injury, or lack of lubrication that resolves isn't the disorder, but it's still worth treating.
hope_note: This is one of the most treatable sexual problems. Many women go from 'impossible' to comfortable with the right team.

content_notes: Sex-positive, shame-free wording; no explicit technique descriptions. Medication named only in general terms.
Pain after sexual trauma is acknowledged in related topics; trauma-informed wording.
